items.title: superqt
items.text:
"Missing" widgets and components for PyQt and PySide.

superqt is a collection of Qt widgets and utilities that the QtWidgets module doesn't provide: range sliders, sliders for floats, searchable combo boxes and lists, collapsible sections, font and SVG icons, tools for threading and for throttling signals, and more. It is built on qtpy, so the same code works with PyQt5, PyQt6, and PySide6.

Widgets Utilities

items.title: Installation
items.text:
pipuvconda 
pip install superqt

uv add superqt

conda install -c conda-forge superqt

superqt doesn't install a Qt binding. If your environment doesn't have one yet, install one with an extra:

pip install "superqt[pyqt6]"  # or [pyqt5], or [pyside6]

Some features need extra dependencies, which can also be installed as extras:

Extra Installs Needed for cmap cmap QColormapComboBox, CmapCatalogComboBox, colormap utilities quantity pint QQuantity iconify pyconify QIconifyIcon font-fa5, font-fa6 Font Awesome 5 or 6 font icons font-mi6, font-mi7 Material Design Icons 6 or 7 font icons

superqt is tested on macOS, Windows, and Linux, with Python 3.11 and later, and with PyQt5 (5.15), PyQt6, and PySide6.

items.title: Sliders not dragging properly on macOS 12+
items.text:
With Qt 5 on macOS 12 (Monterey) and later, a bug in Qt makes all sliders, including Qt's own, respond badly to dragging (QTBUG-98093, and superqt#74). Qt 6 doesn't have this bug.

superqt includes a workaround: a style sheet for the sliders. It isn't perfect, and it replaces the sliders' styles (so it may interfere with your own; and if you already style your sliders, you may not see the bug). To use it, do one of the following:

  • Set the environment variable USE_MAC_SLIDER_PATCH=1 before importing superqt. superqt's sliders then use the style sheet if they run with Qt 5 on macOS 12 or later (so it's safe to set on other platforms). This applies to all of them except QLabeledSlider, which contains a plain QSlider.
  • Call the applyMacStylePatch() method of a QDoubleSlider, QRangeSlider, or QDoubleRangeSlider. This applies the style sheet whatever the platform, and replaces the slider's style sheet.

  • Apply the style sheet yourself, to any slider:

    from superqt.sliders import MONTEREY_SLIDER_STYLES_FIX

slider.setStyleSheet(MONTEREY_SLIDER_STYLES_FIX)

items.title: Colormap utilities
items.text: The building blocks of the colormap widgets (QColormapComboBox, CmapCatalogComboBox, and QColormapLineEdit), for drawing cmap colormaps elsewhere. They need the cmap extra (pip install "superqt[cmap]").

items.title: draw_colormap
items.text:
draw_colormap(
    painter_or_device: QPainter | QPaintDevice,
    cmap: Colormap | ColorStopsLike,
    rect: QRect | QRectF | None = None,
    border_color: QColor | str | None = None,
    border_width: int = 1,
    lighter: int = 100,
    checkerboard_size: int = 4,
) -> None

Draw a colormap onto a QPainter or QPaintDevice.

Parameters:

  • painter_or_device (QPainter | QPaintDevice) –

    A QPainter instance or a QPaintDevice (e.g. a QWidget or QPixmap) onto which to paint the colormap.

  • cmap (Colormap | Any) –

    cmap.Colormap instance, or anything that can be converted to one (such as a string name of a colormap in the cmap catalog). https://cmap-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/colormaps/#colormaplike-objects

  • rect (QRect | QRectF | None, default: None ) –

    A rect onto which to draw. If None, the painter.viewport() will be used. by default None

  • border_color (QColor | str | None, default: None ) –

    If not None, a border of color border_color and width border_width is included around the edge, by default None.

  • border_width (int, default: 1 ) –

    The width of the border to draw (provided border_color is not None), by default 2

  • lighter (int, default: 100 ) –

    Percentage by which to lighten (or darken) the colors. Greater than 100 lightens, less than 100 darkens, by default 100 (i.e. no change).

  • checkerboard_size (bool, default: 4 ) –

    Size (in pixels) of the checkerboard pattern to draw, by default 5. If 0, no checkerboard is drawn.

Examples:

from qtpy.QtGui import QPixmap
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QWidget
from superqt.utils import draw_colormap

viridis = "viridis"  # or cmap.Colormap('viridis')


class W(QWidget):
    def paintEvent(self, event) -> None:
        draw_colormap(self, viridis, event.rect())


# or draw onto a QPixmap
pm = QPixmap(200, 200)
draw_colormap(pm, viridis)

items.title: CodeSyntaxHighlight
items.text: A QSyntaxHighlighter that highlights code in a QTextEdit (or any QTextDocument), using Pygments. It takes the name of a language and of a style, which can be changed later with setLanguage and setTheme.

items.title: Example
items.text:
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QTextEdit

from superqt.utils import CodeSyntaxHighlight

app = QApplication([])

text_area = QTextEdit()
# (given the QTextEdit, rather than its document, it also sets the background)
highlight = CodeSyntaxHighlight(text_area, "python", "monokai")
text_area.setPlainText(
    """from argparse import ArgumentParser

def main():
    parser = ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("name", help="Your name")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(f"Hello {args.name}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"""
)
text_area.resize(400, 200)
text_area.show()

app.exec()

Subclass of QSyntaxHighlighter

CodeSyntaxHighlight inherits all of QSyntaxHighlighter's methods, signals, and properties. Only those that superqt adds or changes are listed here.

CodeSyntaxHighlight(
    parent: SupportsDocumentAndPalette
    | QTextDocument
    | QObject
    | None,
    lang: str,
    theme: KnownStyle | str = "default",

A syntax highlighter for code using Pygments.

Parameters:

  • parent (QTextDocument | QObject | None) –

    The parent object. Usually a QTextDocument. To use this class with a QTextArea, pass in text_area.document().

  • lang (str) –

    The language of the code to highlight. This should be a string that Pygments recognizes, e.g. 'python', 'pytb', 'cpp', 'java', etc.

  • theme (KnownStyle | str, default: 'default' ) –

    The name of the Pygments style to use. For a complete list of available styles, use pygments.styles.get_all_styles().

Examples:

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QTextEdit
from superqt.utils import CodeSyntaxHighlight

text_area = QTextEdit()
highlighter = CodeSyntaxHighlight(text_area.document(), "python", "monokai")

# then manually apply the background color to the text area.
palette = text_area.palette()
bgrd_color = QColor(self._highlight.background_color)
palette.setColor(QPalette.ColorRole.Base, bgrd_color)
text_area.setPalette(palette)

items.title: Showing exceptions in a dialog
items.text: exceptions_as_dialog is a context manager that catches exceptions raised in its block, and shows them in a QMessageBox (or a QErrorMessage, which lets the user hide messages they've seen), instead of letting them propagate.

items.title: exceptions_as_dialog
items.text:
exceptions_as_dialog(
    exceptions: type[BaseException]
    | tuple[type[BaseException], ...] = Exception,
    icon: Icon = Critical,
    title: str = "An error occurred",
    msg_template: str = "{exc_value}",
    buttons: StandardButton = Ok,
    parent: QWidget | None = None,
    flags: WindowType = _DEFAULT_FLAGS,
    use_error_message: bool | QErrorMessage = False,
)

Context manager that shows a dialog when an exception is raised.

See examples below for common usage patterns.

To determine whether an exception was raised or not, check the exception attribute after the context manager has exited. If use_error_message is False (the default), you can also access the dialog attribute to get/manipulate the QMessageBox instance.

Parameters:

  • exceptions (type[BaseException] | tuple[type[BaseException], ...], default: Exception ) –

    The exception(s) to catch, by default Exception (i.e. all exceptions).

  • icon (Icon, default: Critical ) –

    The icon to show in the QMessageBox, by default QMessageBox.Icon.Critical

  • title (str, default: 'An error occurred' ) –

    The title of the QMessageBox, by default "An error occurred".

  • msg_template (str, default: '{exc_value}' ) –

    The message to show in the QMessageBox. The message will be formatted using three variables:

    • exc_value: the exception instance
    • exc_type: the exception type
    • tb: the traceback as a string

    The default template is the content of the exception: "{exc_value}"

  • buttons (StandardButton, default: Ok ) –

    The buttons to show in the QMessageBox, by default QMessageBox.StandardButton.Ok

  • parent (QWidget | None, default: None ) –

    The parent widget of the QMessageBox, by default None

  • use_error_message (bool | QErrorMessage, default: False ) –

    Whether to use a QErrorMessage instead of a QMessageBox. By default False. QErrorMessage shows a checkbox that the user can check to prevent seeing the message again (based on the text of the formatted msg_template.) If True, the global QMessageError.qtHandler() instance is used to maintain a history of dismissed messages. You may also pass a QErrorMessage instance to use a specific instance. If use_error_message is True, or if you pass your own QErrorMessage instance, the parent argument is ignored.

Attributes:

  • dialog (QMessageBox | None) –

    The QMessageBox instance that was created (if use_error_message was False). This can be used, among other things, to determine the result of the dialog (e.g. dialog.result()) or to manipulate the dialog (e.g. dialog.setDetailedText("some text")).

  • exception (BaseException | None) –

    Will hold the exception instance if an exception was raised and caught.

Examples:

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication
from superqt.utils import exceptions_as_dialog

app = QApplication([])

with exceptions_as_dialog() as ctx:
    raise Exception("This will be caught and shown in a QMessageBox")

# you can access the exception instance here
assert ctx.exception is not None

# with exceptions_as_dialog(ValueError):
#     1 / 0  # ZeroDivisionError is not caught, so this will raise

with exceptions_as_dialog(msg_template="Error: {exc_value}"):
    raise Exception("This message will be inserted at 'exc_value'")

for _i in range(3):
    with exceptions_as_dialog(AssertionError, use_error_message=True):
        assert False, "Uncheck the checkbox to ignore this in the future"

# use ctx.dialog to get the result of the dialog
btns = QMessageBox.StandardButton.Ok | QMessageBox.StandardButton.Cancel
with exceptions_as_dialog(buttons=btns) as ctx:
    raise Exception("This will be caught and shown in a QMessageBox")
print(ctx.dialog.result())  # prints which button was clicked

app.exec()  # needed only for the use_error_message example to show

items.title: QMessageHandler
items.text: A context manager that captures the messages that Qt logs (with qDebug, qWarning, qCritical, and so on), instead of printing them, for example to check for them in tests, or to send them to Python's logging.

items.title: QMessageHandler
items.text:
QMessageHandler(logger: Logger | None = None)

A context manager to intercept messages from Qt.

Parameters:

  • logger (Logger, default: None ) –

    If provided, intercepted messages will be logged with logger at the corresponding python log level, by default None

Attributes:

  • records (list of tuple) –

    Captured messages. This is a 3-tuple of: (log_level: int, message: str, context: dict)

Examples:

>>> handler = QMessageHandler()
>>> handler.install()  # now all Qt output will be available at mh.records

>>> with QMessageHandler() as handler:  # temporarily install
...     ...

>>> logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
>>> with QMessageHandler(logger):  # re-route Qt messages to a python logger.
...     ...

items.title: Blocking signals
items.text:
signals_blocked blocks the signals of one or more QObjects while its block runs, and restores each object's previous state afterwards (like QSignalBlocker, as a context manager):

from superqt.utils import signals_blocked

with signals_blocked(slider):
    slider.setValue(10)  # doesn't emit valueChanged

items.title: Threading decorators
items.text:
Qt objects must generally be used from the thread they live in, and widgets from the main (GUI) thread. These two decorators make a function run in the right thread, whichever thread calls it:

ensure_main_thread Runs the decorated function, or method, in the main thread. ensure_object_thread Runs the decorated method of a QObject in the thread that the object lives in (see Qt's threads and QObjects).

They're meant for calling Qt code from code that doesn't use Qt (such as a callback from another library's thread). Between Qt objects, signals and slots already do this.

items.title: Usage
items.text:
When called from another thread, the decorated function is queued to run in its target thread, and the call returns a concurrent.futures.Future at once. (When called from the target thread, the function runs right away, and the Future it returns is already done.)

from qtpy.QtCore import QObject

from superqt import ensure_main_thread, ensure_object_thread


@ensure_main_thread
def update_label(text):
    print("this runs in the main thread")


class Counter(QObject):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self._value = 1

    @ensure_main_thread
    def show(self):
        print("this runs in the main thread")

    @ensure_object_thread
    def reset(self):
        print("this runs in the thread that the Counter lives in")

    @property
    def value(self):
        return self._value

    @value.setter
    @ensure_object_thread
    def value(self, value):
        print("setters work too")
        self._value = value

items.title: Waiting for the result
items.text:
To wait for the function to finish, and get its return value, pass await_return=True. It waits for at most timeout milliseconds (1000 by default), and then raises a TimeoutError.

Warning

The calling thread is blocked while it waits.

from concurrent.futures import Future

from superqt import ensure_main_thread


@ensure_main_thread
def get_one():
    return 1


@ensure_main_thread(await_return=True)
def get_two():
    return 2


@ensure_main_thread(await_return=True, timeout=10000)
def get_three():
    return 3


assert isinstance(get_one(), Future)
assert get_two() == 2
assert get_three() == 3

items.title: Thread workers
items.text:
Workers run a long task in another thread, so that the GUI stays responsive, and report back with signals (such as started, returned, errored, finished, and, for generators, yielded), which can safely update the GUI from the main thread. Except for new_worker_qthread, they use Qt's QRunnable and global QThreadPool.

The simplest way to use them is the @thread_worker decorator. Calling a decorated function returns a worker, which runs the function when it's started (or at once, if callbacks are given with connect=):

import time

from superqt.utils import thread_worker


@thread_worker
def long_task(n):
    time.sleep(n)
    return n


worker = long_task(2)
worker.returned.connect(print)
worker.start()

If the function is a generator, the worker is a GeneratorWorker: it emits yielded for each value, and can be paused, resumed, and aborted between them. Otherwise, it's a FunctionWorker.

These tools were written for napari, and moved to superqt. The napari guide to threading describes them in more depth.

items.title: run
items.text:
run() -> None

Start the worker.

The end-user should never need to call this function. But it cannot be made private or renamed, since it is called by Qt.

The order of method calls when starting a worker is:

   calls QThreadPool.globalInstance().start(worker)
   |               triggered by the QThreadPool.start() method
   |               |             called by worker.run
   |               |             |
   V               V             V
   worker.start -> worker.run -> worker.work

This is the function that actually gets called when calling QThreadPool.start(worker). It simply wraps the work() method, and emits a few signals. Subclasses should NOT override this method (except with good reason), and instead should implement work().

items.title: work
items.text:
work() -> Exception | _R

Main method to execute the worker.

The end-user should never need to call this function. But subclasses must implement this method (See GeneratorFunction.work for an example implementation). Minimally, it should check self.abort_requested periodically and exit if True.

Examples:

class MyWorker(WorkerBase):
    def work(self):
        i = 0
        while True:
            if self.abort_requested:
                self.aborted.emit()
                break
            i += 1
            if i > max_iters:
                break
            time.sleep(0.5)

The order of method calls when starting a worker is:

items.title: await_workers
items.text:
await_workers(msecs: int | None = None) -> None

Ask all workers to quit, and wait up to msec for quit.

Attempts to clean up all running workers by calling worker.quit() method. Any workers in the WorkerBase._worker_set set will have this method.

By default, this function will block indefinitely, until worker threads finish. If a timeout is provided, a RuntimeError will be raised if the workers do not gracefully exit in the time requests, but the threads will NOT be killed. It is (currently) left to the user to use their OS to force-quit rogue threads.

Important

If the user does not put any yields in their function, and the function is super long, it will just hang... For instance, there's no graceful way to kill this thread in python:

@thread_worker
def ZZZzzz():
    time.sleep(10000000)

This is why it's always advisable to use a generator that periodically yields for long-running computations in another thread.

See this stack-overflow post for a good discussion on the difficulty of killing a rogue python thread:

Parameters:

    Waits up to msecs milliseconds for all threads to exit and removes all threads from the thread pool. If msecs is None (the default), the timeout is ignored (waits for the last thread to exit).

Raises:

  • RuntimeError –

    If a timeout is provided and workers do not quit successfully within the time allotted.

Decorator that runs a function in a separate thread when called.

When called, the decorated function returns a WorkerBase. See create_worker for additional keyword arguments that can be used when calling the function.

The returned worker will have these signals:

  • started: emitted when the work is started
  • finished: emitted when the work is finished
  • returned: emitted with return value
  • errored: emitted with error object on Exception

It will also have a worker.start() method that can be used to start execution of the function in another thread. (useful if you need to connect callbacks to signals prior to execution)

If the decorated function is a generator, the returned worker will also provide these signals:

  • yielded: emitted with yielded values
  • paused: emitted when a running job has successfully paused
  • resumed: emitted when a paused job has successfully resumed
  • aborted: emitted when a running job is successfully aborted

And these methods:

  • quit: ask the thread to quit
  • toggle_paused: toggle the running state of the thread.
  • send: send a value into the generator. (This requires that your decorator function uses the value = yield syntax)

    Function to call in another thread. For communication between threads may be a generator function.

  • start_thread (bool, default: None ) –

    Whether to immediaetly start the thread. If False, the returned worker must be manually started with worker.start(). by default it will be False if the _connect argument is None, otherwise True.

  • connect (Dict[str, Union[Callable, Sequence]], default: None ) –

    The WorkerBase to instantiate, by default FunctionWorker will be used if func is a regular function, and GeneratorWorker will be used if it is a generator.

    function that creates a worker, puts it in a new thread and returns the worker instance.

    i = start
    while i <= end:
        time.sleep(0.1)
        yield i

    # do teardown

# `connect` argument in the `@thread_worker` decorator... in which
# case the worker will start immediately when long_function() is called

    @Slot()

        import time

        for i in range(10):
            time.sleep(1)
            self.increment.emit(i)
        self.finished.emit()

items.title: Throttling and debouncing
items.text:
When a function is called many times in quick succession (for example, by a slider's valueChanged signal while it's dragged), throttling and debouncing limit how often it actually runs:

  • Throttling runs it at most once per timeout. With the default (leading) policy, the first call runs at once, and further calls during the timeout are combined into one call at its end.
  • Debouncing waits until the calls have stopped for the timeout, and then runs it once.

Below, a slider's valueChanged signal is connected to a function directly, and to the same function decorated with qthrottled and with qdebounced. Each tick is a call, and the value is what the last call received:

The code for this demo 
"""A slider's valueChanged, connected directly, throttled, and debounced.

Drag the slider: each lane of the timeline draws a tick for each call (newest on
the right), and shows the value that the last call received. (Inspired by
examples/throttler_demo.py, which is adapted from KDAB's KDToolBox.)
"""

import time
from collections import deque

from qtpy.QtCore import QPointF, QRectF, QSize, Qt, QTimer
from qtpy.QtGui import QColor, QPainter, QPen
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QSlider, QVBoxLayout, QWidget

from superqt.utils import qdebounced, qthrottled

SPEED = 100  # pixels per second
LABEL_WIDTH = 170


class Timeline(QWidget):
    """Lanes of ticks that scroll to the left, one lane per kind of call."""

    def __init__(self, lanes: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._colors = lanes  # lane name -> tick color
        self._ticks = {name: deque() for name in lanes}
        self._values = dict.fromkeys(lanes, "")
        self._timer = QTimer(self, interval=16, timeout=self.update)
        self._timer.start()

    def sizeHint(self) -> QSize:
        return QSize(480, 150)

    def add(self, lane: str, value: int) -> None:
        self._ticks[lane].append(time.perf_counter())
        self._values[lane] = str(value)

    def paintEvent(self, event) -> None:
        painter = QPainter(self)
        painter.setRenderHint(QPainter.RenderHint.Antialiasing)
        palette = self.palette()
        painter.fillRect(self.rect(), palette.base())
        now, height = time.perf_counter(), self.height() / len(self._ticks)
        for i, (lane, ticks) in enumerate(self._ticks.items()):
            top = i * height
            # the lane's name, and the last value it received
            painter.setPen(palette.text().color())
            label = QRectF(10, top, LABEL_WIDTH - 20, height)
            align = Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignLeft | Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignVCenter
            painter.drawText(label, align, f"{lane}\n{self._values[lane]}")
            # a tick for each call
            painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(self._colors[lane]), 2))
            for t in ticks:
                x = self.width() - (now - t) * SPEED
                painter.drawLine(QPointF(x, top + 8), QPointF(x, top + height - 8))
            while ticks and self.width() - (now - ticks[0]) * SPEED < LABEL_WIDTH:
                ticks.popleft()


app = QApplication([])

window = QWidget()
slider = QSlider(Qt.Orientation.Horizontal)
slider.setValue(20)
timeline = Timeline(
    {
        "valueChanged": "#8c8c8c",
        "qthrottled (100 ms)": "#3b82f6",
        "qdebounced (300 ms)": "#f59e0b",
    }
)
layout = QVBoxLayout(window)
layout.addWidget(slider)
layout.addWidget(timeline)


@qthrottled(timeout=100)
def throttled(value: int) -> None:
    timeline.add("qthrottled (100 ms)", value)


@qdebounced(timeout=300)
def debounced(value: int) -> None:
    timeline.add("qdebounced (300 ms)", value)


slider.valueChanged.connect(lambda value: timeline.add("valueChanged", value))
slider.valueChanged.connect(throttled)
slider.valueChanged.connect(debounced)

window.show()
app.exec()

For more background, see Debouncing and throttling explained.

The qthrottled and qdebounced decorators wrap a function:

from superqt.utils import qdebounced, qthrottled


@qthrottled(timeout=100)  # milliseconds
def update_preview(value): ...


@qdebounced(timeout=300)
def save_settings(value): ...


slider.valueChanged.connect(update_preview)
slider.valueChanged.connect(save_settings)

The decorated function is called with the arguments of the last call that it combined. The QSignalThrottler and QSignalDebouncer objects do the same for signals: connect a signal to their throttle() slot, and their triggered signal is emitted at the throttled (or debounced) rate:

from superqt.utils import QSignalThrottler

throttler = QSignalThrottler()
throttler.setTimeout(100)
slider.valueChanged.connect(throttler.throttle)
throttler.triggered.connect(update_view)

items.title: Icons
items.text:
superqt can create a QIcon from an icon library in two ways:

  • QIconifyIcon uses the SVG icons of Iconify: over 450,000 icons, from more than 260 icon sets (including Bootstrap Icons, Font Awesome, and Material Design Icons). It's the usual choice: any icon is available without choosing an icon set in advance.
  • Font icons (superqt.fonticon) draw the characters of icon fonts that you install as plugins. They work without network access, can be animated, and can be the text of a label or button.

QIconifyIconAny of Iconify's SVG icons, downloaded when first used. Font iconsGlyphs of installed icon fonts, drawn as text.

items.text:
Most of the differences follow from one detail: QIconifyIcon draws SVG images that are downloaded (and cached) the first time they're used, while superqt.fonticon draws the characters of a font file that's installed in advance, as a plugin.

items.title: Font icons
items.text:
superqt.fonticon creates QIcons from the characters (glyphs) of icon fonts, such as Font Awesome or Material Design Icons. Icon fonts are installed as plugins: superqt doesn't come with any.

Compared with QIconifyIcon, font icons don't need network access, can be animated, and can be the text of a label or button (see the comparison).

items.title: Installing a font
items.text:
These icon fonts are available as plugins, and as extras of superqt:

Font Install Browse the icons Font Awesome 6 pip install "superqt[font-fa6]" https://fontawesome.com/v6/search Font Awesome 5 pip install "superqt[font-fa5]" https://fontawesome.com/v5/search Material Design Icons 7 pip install "superqt[font-mi7]" https://pictogrammers.com/library/mdi/ Material Design Icons 6 pip install "superqt[font-mi6]" https://pictogrammers.com/library/mdi/ (shows version 7: see the changes from version 6)

Other fonts are available as separate packages:

  • fonticon-bootstrapicons
  • fonticon-linearicons
  • fonticon-feather

GlyphSearch searches several icon libraries at once. If you'd like to use a font that isn't available as a plugin, please open a feature request.

items.title: Basic example
items.text:
from fonticon_fa5 import FA5S
from qtpy.QtCore import QSize
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QPushButton

from superqt.fonticon import icon

app = QApplication([])

button = QPushButton()
button.setIcon(icon(FA5S.smile, color="royalblue"))
button.setIconSize(QSize(96, 96))
button.show()

app.exec()

Glyphs are named by keys in the form "prefix.name", such as "fa5s.smile", or by the constants of the classes that the plugins provide, such as FA5S.smile, which IDEs autocomplete (and check for typos).

items.title: Colors and states
items.text:
icon takes the color, scale, opacity, and transform of the glyph. Without a color, glyphs are black, whatever the widget's palette: for a dark theme, pass a color (for example, one from the palette).

states gives other options (including another glyph) for other states and modes of the icon. Its keys are a state ("on", "off"), a mode ("normal", "active", "selected", "disabled"), or both (as in "on_disabled"). For example, a red heart when a checkable button is checked:

button.setCheckable(True)
button.setIcon(
    icon(
        FA5S.smile,
        color="gray",
        states={"on": {"glyph_key": FA5S.heart, "color": "red"}},
    )
)

In modes other than normal (such as disabled), a glyph without a color for that mode is adjusted by the style, like any other icon (for example, grayed out when disabled).

items.title: Animations
items.text:
The animation argument of icon() takes an Animation, such as spin or pulse, created with the widget that shows the icon:

from fonticon_fa5 import FA5S
from qtpy.QtGui import QPalette
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QHBoxLayout, QPushButton, QWidget

from superqt.fonticon import icon, pulse, spin

app = QApplication([])

window = QWidget()
layout = QHBoxLayout(window)
color = window.palette().color(QPalette.ColorRole.ButtonText).name()  # (dark themes)

spinning = QPushButton("spin")
spinning.setIcon(icon(FA5S.sync, color=color, animation=spin(spinning)))
layout.addWidget(spinning)

pulsing = QPushButton("pulse")
pulsing.setIcon(icon(FA5S.spinner, color=color, animation=pulse(pulsing)))
layout.addWidget(pulsing)

window.show()
app.exec()

items.title: Glyphs as text
items.text:
setTextIcon makes a glyph the text of a widget, such as a label or a button, by setting its text to the glyph and its font to the icon font. The glyph is then drawn as text, in the widget's text color, so it follows the palette and style sheets:

label = QLabel()
setTextIcon(label, FA5S.smile, size=32)
label.setStyleSheet("color: orange")

font returns the QFont of an icon font (by its prefix, such as "fa5s"), for drawing glyphs yourself.

items.title: Writing a plugin
items.text: Font packages register themselves with the "superqt.fonticon" entry point (superqt.fonticon.ENTRY_POINT), and define their glyphs with an IconFont subclass (whose metaclass, IconFontMeta, turns its attributes into glyph keys). fonticon-cookiecutter is a template for a new one, and the packages above are examples, such as fonticon-fontawesome6. To use a font file without writing a package, see addFont.

items.title: icon
items.text:
icon(
    glyph_key: str,
    scale_factor: float = DEFAULT_SCALING_FACTOR,
    color: ValidColor | None = None,
    opacity: float = 1,
    animation: Animation | None = None,
    transform: QTransform | None = None,
    states: dict[str, IconOptionDict | IconOpts]
    | None = None,
) -> QFontIcon

Create a QIcon for glyph_key, with a number of optional settings.

The glyph_key (e.g. 'fa5s.smile') represents a Font-family & style, and a glyph. In most cases, the key should be provided by a plugin in the environment, like:

  • fonticon-fontawesome5 ('fa5s' & 'fa5r' prefixes)
  • fonticon-materialdesignicons6 ('mdi6' prefix)

...but fonts can also be added manually using addFont.

Parameters:

  • glyph_key (str) –

    String encapsulating a font-family, style, and glyph. e.g. 'fa5s.smile'.

  • scale_factor (float, default: DEFAULT_SCALING_FACTOR ) –

    Scale factor (fraction of widget height), When widget icon is painted on widget, it will use font.setPixelSize(round(wdg.height() * scale_factor)). by default 0.875.

  • color (ValidColor, default: None ) –

    Color for the font, by default None. (e.g. The default QColor) Valid color types include QColor, int, str, Qt.GlobalColor, tuple (of integer: RGB[A]) (anything that can be passed to QColor).

  • opacity (float, default: 1 ) –

    Opacity of icon, by default 1

  • animation (Animation, default: None ) –

    Animation for the icon. A subclass of superqt.fonticon.Animation, that provides a concrete animate method. (see "spin" and "pulse" for examples). by default None.

  • transform (QTransform, default: None ) –

    A QTransform to apply when painting the icon, by default None

  • states (dict, default: None ) –

    Provide additional styling for the icon in different states. states must be a mapping of string to dict, where:

    • the key represents a QIcon.State ("on", "off"), a QIcon.Mode ("normal", "active", "selected", "disabled"), or any combination of a state & mode separated by an underscore (e.g. "off_active", "selected_on", etc...).
    • the value is a dict with all of the same key/value meanings listed above as parameters to this function (e.g. glyph_key, color,scale_factor, animation, etc...)

    Missing keys in the state dicts will be taken from the default options, provided by the parameters above.

Returns:

  • QFontIcon –

    A subclass of QIcon. Can be used wherever QIcons are used, such as widget.setIcon()

Examples:

simple example (using the string 'fa5s.smile' assumes the fonticon-fontawesome5 plugin is installed)

>>> btn = QPushButton()
>>> btn.setIcon(icon("fa5s.smile"))

can also directly import from fonticon_fa5

>>> from fonticon_fa5 import FA5S
>>> btn.setIcon(icon(FA5S.smile))

with animation

>>> btn2 = QPushButton()
>>> btn2.setIcon(icon(FA5S.spinner, animation=pulse(btn2)))

complicated example

>>> btn = QPushButton()
>>> btn.setIcon(
...     icon(
...         FA5S.ambulance,
...         color="blue",
...         states={
...             "active": {
...                 "glyph": FA5S.bath,
...                 "color": "red",
...                 "scale_factor": 0.5,
...                 "animation": pulse(btn),
...             },
...             "disabled": {
...                 "color": "green",
...                 "scale_factor": 0.8,
...                 "animation": spin(btn),
...             },
...         },
...     )
... )
>>> btn.setIconSize(QSize(256, 256))
>>> btn.show()

items.title: addFont
items.text:
addFont(
    filepath: str,
    prefix: str,
    charmap: dict[str, str] | None = None,
) -> tuple[str, str] | None

Add OTF/TTF file at filepath to the registry under prefix.

If you'd like to later use a fontkey in the form of prefix.some-name, then charmap must be provided and provide a mapping for all of the glyph names to their unicode numbers. If a charmap is not provided, glyphs must be directly accessed with their unicode as something like key.￿.

Note

in most cases, users will not need this. Instead, they should install a font plugin, like:

  • fonticon-fontawesome5
  • fonticon-materialdesignicons6

Parameters:

  • filepath (str) –

    Path to an OTF or TTF file containing the fonts

  • prefix (str) –

    A prefix that will represent this font file when used for lookup. For example, 'fa5s' for 'Font-Awesome 5 Solid'.

  • charmap (Dict[str, str], default: None ) –

    optional mapping for all of the glyph names to their unicode numbers. See note above.

Returns:

  • (Tuple[str, str], optional) –

    font-family and font-style for the file just registered, or None if something goes wrong.

items.title: IconFont
items.text:
Helper class that provides a standard way to create an IconFont.

Examples:

class FA5S(IconFont):
    __font_file__ = '...'
    some_char = 0xfa42

items.title: IconFontMeta
items.text:
IconFont metaclass.

This updates the value of all class attributes to be prefaced with the class name (lowercase), and makes sure that all values are valid characters.

Examples:

This metaclass turns the following class:

class FA5S(metaclass=IconFontMeta):
    __font_file__ = 'path/to/font.otf'
    some_char = 0xfa42

into this:

class FA5S:
    __font_file__ = path/to/font.otf'
    some_char = 'fa5s.既'

In usage, this means that someone could use icon(FA5S.some_char) (provided that the FA5S class/namespace has already been registered). This makes IDE attribute checking and autocompletion easier.

items.title: QIconifyIcon
items.text:
A QIcon with one of the SVG icons of Iconify: over 450,000 icons, from more than 260 open source icon sets. Find an icon at https://icon-sets.iconify.design, and create it with its key, in the form "prefix:name": QIconifyIcon("bi:bell"). (For a comparison with font icons, see Icons.)

Requires pyconify

Icons are downloaded with pyconify, which you can install with the iconify extra:

pip install "superqt[iconify]"

items.title: Example
items.text:
from qtpy.QtCore import QSize
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QPushButton

from superqt import QIconifyIcon

app = QApplication([])

btn = QPushButton()
btn.setIcon(QIconifyIcon("fluent-emoji-flat:alarm-clock"))
btn.setIconSize(QSize(60, 60))
btn.show()

app.exec()

items.title: Colors, rotation, and states
items.text:
Single-color icons can be colored, and any icon can be flipped or rotated:

button.setIcon(QIconifyIcon("bi:bell-fill", color="red", rotate=90))

Without a color, single-color icons are black, whatever the widget's palette. For a dark theme, pass a color, for example one from the palette:

color = button.palette().color(QPalette.ColorRole.ButtonText).name()
button.setIcon(QIconifyIcon("bi:bell", color=color))

addKey adds icons for other states and modes of the same QIcon. For example, a different icon when a checkable button is checked:

icon = QIconifyIcon("bi:bell", color="gray")
icon.addKey("bi:bell-fill", color="orange", state=QIcon.State.On)
button.setCheckable(True)
button.setIcon(icon)

items.title: How icons are fetched
items.text:
The first time an icon is used, pyconify downloads it from the Iconify API (api.iconify.design), and saves it in a cache on disk, where later sessions find it.

  • The download happens when the QIconifyIcon is created, in the thread that creates it, which waits for it (with a timeout of 2 seconds).
  • The first icon of each session also asks the API when the icon sets last changed, so that cached icons that are out of date are downloaded again.
  • Without network access, cached icons still load. An icon that isn't cached causes a warning, and is replaced by a question mark icon.
  • pyconify.get_cache_directory() returns the location of the cache. To use another directory, set the PYCONIFY_CACHE environment variable to it (or to 0, to turn the cache off) before superqt.iconify (or pyconify) is imported.

items.title: Using icons offline, or in an app
items.text:
To make sure that an app's icons are available without network access, ship them in a cache directory:

  1. Fill a directory with the icons: create each of them once (for example, by running the app), with PYCONIFY_CACHE set to that directory.

  2. Ship the directory with the app, and set PYCONIFY_CACHE to it before importing superqt.iconify:

    import os
from pathlib import Path

os.environ["PYCONIFY_CACHE"] = str(Path(__file__).parent / "icon_cache")

from superqt import QIconifyIcon

The icons are then loaded from the directory. With network access, an icon whose set has changed since is downloaded again, into the same directory (so it should be writable).

items.title: Licenses
items.text: Each icon set has its own license. Most are permissive (such as MIT or Apache 2.0), but many require attribution (CC BY 4.0), and a few are GPL. The license of a set is shown on its page at https://icon-sets.iconify.design, and returned by pyconify.collections().

items.title: QIconifyIcon
items.text:
QIconifyIcon(
    *key: str,
    color: str | None = None,
    flip: Flip | None = None,
    rotate: Rotation | None = None,
    dir: str | None = None,
)

QIcon backed by an iconify icon.

Iconify includes over 450,000 icons from 260+ icon sets, including Bootstrap, Font Awesome, Material Design, and many more.

Search available icons at https://icon-sets.iconify.design Once you find one you like, use the key in the format "prefix:name" to create an icon: QIconifyIcon("bi:bell").

This class is a thin wrapper around the pyconify svg_path function. It pulls SVGs from iconify, creates a temporary SVG file and uses it as the source for a QIcon. SVGs are cached to disk, and persist across sessions (until pyconify.clear_cache() is called).

Parameters are the same as QIconifyIcon.addKey, which can be used to add additional icons for various modes and states to the same QIcon.

Parameters:

  • *key (str, default: () ) –

    Icon set prefix and name. May be passed as a single string in the format "prefix:name" or as two separate strings: 'prefix', 'name'.

  • color (str, default: None ) –

    Icon color. If not provided, the icon will appear black (the icon fill color will be set to the string "currentColor").

  • flip (str, default: None ) –

    Flip icon. Must be one of "horizontal", "vertical", "horizontal,vertical"

  • rotate (str | int, default: None ) –

    Rotate icon. Must be one of 0, 90, 180, 270, or 0, 1, 2, 3 (equivalent to 0, 90, 180, 270, respectively)

  • dir (str, default: None ) –

    If 'dir' is not None, the file will be created in that directory, otherwise a default directory is used.

Examples:

>>> from qtpy.QtWidgets import QPushButton
>>> from superqt import QIconifyIcon
>>> btn = QPushButton()
>>> icon = QIconifyIcon("bi:alarm-fill", color="red", rotate=90)
>>> btn.setIcon(icon)

items.title: CmapCatalogComboBox
items.text:
A QComboBox with every colormap in the cmap catalog. Typing in it shows the colormaps whose names contain the text, and currentColormap() returns a cmap.Colormap.

Requires cmap

Colormaps come from the cmap library, which you can install with the cmap extra:

pip install "superqt[cmap]"

The categories and interpolation keyword arguments limit the colormaps to those in some categories (such as "sequential"), or with one interpolation (such as "linear"). By default, colormaps are listed by their short names, and by their full names (namespace:name) only where two namespaces use the same short name; pass prefer_short_names=False to always use full names.

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt.cmap import CmapCatalogComboBox

app = QApplication([])

catalog_combo = CmapCatalogComboBox(interpolation="linear")
catalog_combo.setCurrentText("viridis")
catalog_combo.show()

app.exec()

Subclass of QComboBox

CmapCatalogComboBox inherits all of QComboBox's methods, signals, and properties. Only those that superqt adds or changes are listed here.

items.title: QCollapsible
items.text:
A QFrame with a header button that hides or shows its contents, with an animation. Add contents with addWidget.

  • expand() and collapse() open and close it from code (pass animate=False to skip the animation), and toggled emits True or False when it opens or closes.
  • setExpandedIcon and setCollapsedIcon change the header's icons (a QIcon, or a string such as "▼"), and setDuration and setEasingCurve change the animation.
  • setLocked(True) keeps it from opening or closing, until it's unlocked.
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication, QLabel, QPushButton

from superqt import QCollapsible

app = QApplication([])

collapsible = QCollapsible("Advanced analysis")
collapsible.addWidget(QLabel("This is the inside of the collapsible frame"))
for i in range(4):
    collapsible.addWidget(QPushButton(f"Content button {i + 1}"))

collapsible.expand(animate=False)
collapsible.show()
app.exec()

Subclass of QFrame

QCollapsible inherits all of QFrame's methods, signals, and properties. Only those that superqt adds or changes are listed here.

items.title: QColorComboBox
items.text:
A QComboBox for choosing a color from a list. Colors can be given as anything that QColor accepts (names, hex strings, QColors, and so on); currentColor() returns a QColor, and currentColorChanged emits one.

  • With setUserColorsAllowed(True) (or allow_user_colors=True), an "Add Color..." item at the end of the list opens a QColorDialog, and adds the chosen color.
  • setInvalidColorPolicy sets what happens when an invalid color is added: it's ignored (InvalidColorPolicy.Ignore, the default), or it causes a warning (Warn) or an exception (Raise).
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QColorComboBox

app = QApplication([])

colors = QColorComboBox()
colors.addColors(["red", "green", "blue"])

# show an "Add Color" item that opens a QColorDialog when clicked
colors.setUserColorsAllowed(True)

# emits a QColor when changed
colors.currentColorChanged.connect(print)
colors.show()

app.exec()

items.title: QColormapComboBox
items.text:
A QComboBox for choosing a colormap from a list. Each item shows the colormap, and currentColormap() returns a cmap.Colormap.

Requires cmap

Colormaps come from the cmap library, which you can install with the cmap extra:

pip install "superqt[cmap]"

Colormaps can be added in any of the forms that cmap accepts: the name of a colormap in its catalog, a sequence of colors (which are interpolated), a cmap.Colormap, and others.

  • Typing in the combo box filters the colormaps (turn this off with setFilterable(False)).
  • With setUserAdditionsAllowed(True) (or allow_user_colormaps=True), an "Add Colormap..." item at the end of the list opens a dialog for choosing any colormap in the cmap catalog.
  • Right-clicking an item in the list shows a menu for removing it.

items.title: Example
items.text:
from cmap import Colormap
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QColormapComboBox

app = QApplication([])

# (allow_user_colormaps adds an "Add Colormap..." item, to choose from the catalog)
cmap_combo = QColormapComboBox(allow_user_colormaps=True)
# see note above about colormap-like objects
# as names from the cmap catalog
cmap_combo.addColormaps(["viridis", "plasma", "magma", "gray"])
# as a sequence of colors, linearly interpolated
cmap_combo.addColormap(("#0f0", "slateblue", "#F3A003A0"))
# as a `cmap.Colormap` instance with custom name:
cmap_combo.addColormap(Colormap(("green", "white", "orange"), name="MyMap"))

cmap_combo.show()
app.exec()

items.title: Customizing the appearance
items.text:
By default, the colormap fills about a third of the combo box, next to its name, and all of the width of the items in the list. Both can be changed.

To make the colormap fill the whole width of the combo box:

cmap_combo.lineEdit().setFractionalColormapWidth(1)

(The line edit is a QColormapLineEdit.)

To make the colormaps in the list fill a third of their width:

from superqt.cmap import QColormapItemDelegate

delegate = QColormapItemDelegate(fractional_colormap_width=0.33)
cmap_combo.setItemDelegate(delegate)

items.title: QColormapLineEdit
items.text:
A QLineEdit that shows the colormap named by its text, as you type: a swatch next to the name, or, if fractional_colormap_width is more than 0.75, behind it. When the text isn't the name of a colormap in the cmap catalog, it shows a fallback colormap (gray, by default), and a question mark icon next to the name (unless the swatch is behind it). It's the line edit of QColormapComboBox and CmapCatalogComboBox.

Requires cmap

Colormaps come from the cmap library, which you can install with the cmap extra:

pip install "superqt[cmap]"

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt.cmap import QColormapLineEdit

app = QApplication([])

line_edit = QColormapLineEdit()
line_edit.setText("viridis")
line_edit.show()

app.exec()

With allow_invalid=False, text that isn't a colormap is replaced when editing finishes: by the first completion of the line edit's completer, if it has one, or else by the last valid colormap.

QColormapLineEdit(
    parent: QWidget | None = None,
    *,
    fractional_colormap_width: float = 0.35,
    fallback_cmap: Colormap | str | None = "gray",
    missing_icon: QIcon | StandardPixmap = MISSING,
    checkerboard_size: int = 4,
    allow_invalid: bool = True,
)

A QLineEdit that shows a colormap swatch.

When the current text is a valid colormap name from the cmap package, a swatch of the colormap will be shown to the left of the text (if fractionalColormapWidth is less than .75) or behind the text (for when the colormap fills the full width).

If the current text is not a valid colormap name, a swatch of the fallback colormap will be shown instead (by default, a gray colormap) if fractionalColormapWidth is less than .75.

Parameters:

  • parent (QWidget, default: None ) –

    The parent widget.

  • fractional_colormap_width (float, default: 0.35 ) –

    The fraction of the widget width to use for the colormap swatch. If the colormap is full width (greater than 0.75), the swatch will be drawn behind the text. Otherwise, the swatch will be drawn to the left of the text. Default is 0.33.

  • fallback_cmap (Colormap | str | None, default: 'gray' ) –

    The colormap to use when the current text is not a recognized colormap. by default "gray".

  • missing_icon (QIcon | StandardPixmap, default: MISSING ) –

    The icon to show when the current text is not a recognized colormap and fractionalColormapWidth is less than .75. Default is a question mark.

  • checkerboard_size (int, default: 4 ) –

    Size (in pixels) of the checkerboard pattern to draw behind colormaps with transparency, by default 4. If 0, no checkerboard is drawn.

  • allow_invalid (bool, default: True ) –

    If True, the user can enter any text, even if it does not represent a valid colormap (and fallback_cmap will be shown if it's invalid). If False, the text will be validated when editing is finished or focus is lost, and if the text is not a valid colormap, it will be reverted to the first available valid option from the completer, or, if that's not available, the last valid colormap. Default is True. This is only settable at initialization.

items.title: QElidingLabel
items.text:
A QLabel that elides its text: when the text is too long to fit, its end is replaced with an ellipsis ("…"). text() still returns the full text.

  • setElideMode sets which part of the text is elided (the end, by default; or the start or the middle), with a Qt.TextElideMode.
  • With setWordWrap(True), the text wraps onto as many lines as fit, and only the last line is elided.

For a line edit that does the same, see QElidingLineEdit.

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QElidingLabel

app = QApplication([])

label = QElidingLabel(
    "This text is too long for the label, so the end of it is replaced with an "
    "ellipsis. Make the window wider to see more of it."
)
label.resize(300, 20)
label.show()

app.exec()

line_edit = QElidingLineEdit(

)
line_edit.resize(300, 30)

items.title: QEnumComboBox
items.text:
A QComboBox with the members of a Python Enum as its items. In addition to the QComboBox API, it has:

  • enumClass() and setEnumClass(), to get and set the Enum;
  • currentEnum() and setCurrentEnum(), to get and set the current member;
  • a currentEnumChanged signal, which emits the new member.

Items are shown as str(member) if the Enum defines __str__, and otherwise as the member's name, with underscores replaced by spaces. The items can only come from the Enum: addItem, addItems, insertItem, and insertItems raise a RuntimeError.

from enum import Enum

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QEnumComboBox


class SampleEnum(Enum):
    first = 1
    second = 2
    third = 3


app = QApplication([])

combo = QEnumComboBox()
combo.setEnumClass(SampleEnum)
combo.show()

app.exec()

The Enum can also be passed to the constructor:

# option A:
combo = QEnumComboBox()
combo.setEnumClass(SampleEnum)
# option B:
combo = QEnumComboBox(enum_class=SampleEnum)

items.title: QLabeledRangeSlider
items.text:
A QRangeSlider with labels: one above each handle, with its value, and one at each end, with the minimum and maximum. A value typed into a handle's label moves that handle, and a value typed into an end label changes the minimum or maximum.

  • setHandleLabelPosition moves the handle labels: above (LabelPosition.LabelsAbove, the default), below, on the handles (LabelPosition.LabelsOnHandle), or nowhere (LabelPosition.NoLabel).
  • setEdgeLabelMode sets what the end labels show: the range (EdgeLabelMode.LabelIsRange, the default), the values of the first and last handles (EdgeLabelMode.LabelIsValue; then typing into them moves those handles), or nothing (EdgeLabelMode.NoLabel).
  • With setExpandRangeOnHandleEdit(True), typing a value outside of the range into a handle's label expands the range to include it.
from qtpy.QtCore import Qt
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QLabeledRangeSlider

app = QApplication([])

slider = QLabeledRangeSlider(Qt.Orientation.Horizontal)
slider.setValue((20, 80))
slider.show()

app.exec()

Fine-tuning the label positions

The label_shift_x and label_shift_y attributes offset the handle labels by that many pixels.

items.text:
A spin box for integers of any size. QSpinBox stores its value in a 32-bit integer, so it can't go beyond ±2,147,483,647; QLargeIntSpinBox stores a Python int, and its default maximum is 2**64 - 1.

It doesn't support the prefix, suffix, or special value text of QSpinBox. Its valueChanged signal emits an object (a Python int), because a Qt int couldn't carry large values.

from superqt import QLargeIntSpinBox

app = QApplication([])

spin = QLargeIntSpinBox()
spin.setRange(0, 10**15)
spin.setValue(2**40)  # a QSpinBox can't go above 2**31 - 1
spin.show()

app.exec()

items.title: QRangeSlider
items.text:
A slider with two or more handles, to select a range of values.

from qtpy.QtCore import Qt
from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QRangeSlider

app = QApplication([])

slider = QRangeSlider(Qt.Orientation.Horizontal)
slider.setValue((20, 80))
slider.show()

app.exec()

QRangeSlider is a QSlider, and has the same API, except that value() and sliderPosition() are tuples with one int for each handle (see type changes):

  • The number of handles is the length of the value: slider.setValue([0, 10, 60, 80]) makes four.
  • Handles can be dragged, and so can the bar between the outer handles, which moves all of them. The mouse wheel also moves all of them (with Alt held, it spreads them apart or brings them together).
  • The handles, groove, and ticks are drawn with the platform's style, and can be styled with Qt style sheets (QSS). The color of the bar is the barColor property (qproperty-barColor in QSS).

These methods, in addition to those of QSlider, control the bar between the handles:

Getter Setter Default Description barIsVisible setBarVisible hideBar / showBar True Whether the bar between the handles is shown. barMovesAllHandles setBarMovesAllHandles True Whether clicking on the bar moves all handles, or only the nearest one. barIsRigid setBarIsRigid True Whether the bar keeps its length when it's dragged against the minimum or maximum.

items.title: QSearchableTreeWidget
items.text:
A QTreeWidget that shows a mapping (such as a dict), with a QLineEdit above it to filter it. Nested mappings and sequences become branches of the tree, with keys (or indices) in the first column and values in the second.

The filter is a regular expression: an item is shown if its key or value matches it, or if one of its ancestors' or descendants' does.

Create it with QSearchableTreeWidget.fromData(data). It doesn't watch the mapping for changes: call setData to show new data.

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QSearchableTreeWidget

app = QApplication([])

data = {
    "none": None,
    "str": "test",
    "int": 42,
    "list": [2, 3, 5],
    "dict": {
        "float": 0.5,
        "tuple": (22, 99),
        "bool": False,
    },
}
tree = QSearchableTreeWidget.fromData(data)
tree.tree.expandAll()
tree.show()

app.exec()

QSearchableTreeWidget(parent=None)

A tree widget for showing a mapping that can be searched by key.

This is intended to be used with a read-only mapping and be conveniently created using QSearchableTreeWidget.fromData(data). If the mapping changes, the easiest way to update this is by calling setData.

The tree can be searched by entering a regular expression pattern into the filter line edit. An item is only shown if its, any of its ancestors', or any of its descendants' keys or values match this pattern. The regular expression follows the conventions described by the Qt docs: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qregularexpression.html#details

items.title: QToggleSwitch
items.text:
A checkable QAbstractButton drawn as a toggle switch, with an optional text label. It's used like a QCheckBox: isChecked(), setChecked(), and the toggled signal.

Its colors and size are properties (onColor, offColor, handleColor, switchWidth, switchHeight, and handleSize), so they can also be set in a style sheet, as in QToggleSwitch { qproperty-onColor: red; }. For other looks, subclass it and reimplement drawGroove, drawHandle, or drawText, which are given a superqt.switch.QStyleOptionToggleSwitch with the colors and sizes to use.

from qtpy.QtWidgets import QApplication

from superqt import QToggleSwitch

app = QApplication([])

switch = QToggleSwitch("Notifications")
switch.toggled.connect(print)
switch.show()

app.exec()
